title: What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in streams?
shortTitle: map() vs flatMap() — one-to-one vs one-to-many + flatten

s1_definition.profdef: `map(Function<T,R>)` transforms each element ONE-TO-ONE: each input T produces exactly one output R. `flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>)` transforms each element ONE-TO-MANY and FLATTENS: each input T produces a Stream of R values, and all resulting streams are merged into a single flat Stream<R>. The key difference: map wraps the result (if the function returns a collection, you get `Stream<List<R>>`), flatMap unwraps/flattens it (you get `Stream<R>`).
s1_definition.analogy: **map** is like converting each cheque from dollars to rupees — one cheque in, one cheque out (different value). **flatMap** is like splitting each corporate salary cheque into individual employee cheques — one corporate cheque in, 50 individual cheques out, and they all go on the SAME conveyor belt (flattened). Without flatMap, you'd have 10 bundles of 50 cheques (Stream of Lists). With flatMap, you have 500 individual cheques on one belt (flat Stream).
s1_definition.oneliner: map = 1→1 (wraps). flatMap = 1→many→flatten (unwraps). Use flatMap when map gives you Stream<List<T>> but you want Stream<T>.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `map(Function<T,R>)` transforms each element ONE-TO-ONE: each input T produces exactly one output R. `flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>)` transforms each element ONE-TO-MANY and FLATTENS: each input T produces a Stream of R values, and all resulting streams are merged into a single flat Stream<R>. The key difference: map wraps the result (if the function returns a collection, you get `Stream<List<R>>`), flatMap unwraps/flattens it (you get `Stream<R>`).

| | Signature | Input→Output | Result |
|-|-----------|-------------|--------|
| `map` | `Function<T, R>` | 1 element → 1 element | `Stream<R>` |
| `flatMap` | `Function<T, Stream<R>>` | 1 element → 0,1,many elements | `Stream<R>` (flat) |

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **map** is like converting each cheque from dollars to rupees — one cheque in, one cheque out (different value). **flatMap** is like splitting each corporate salary cheque into individual employee cheques — one corporate cheque in, 50 individual cheques out, and they all go on the SAME conveyor belt (flattened). Without flatMap, you'd have 10 bundles of 50 cheques (Stream of Lists). With flatMap, you have 500 individual cheques on one belt (flat Stream).

**One line to remember:** map = 1→1 (wraps). flatMap = 1→many→flatten (unwraps). Use flatMap when map gives you Stream<List<T>> but you want Stream<T>.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — map.** 3 accounts: SAV2001(3 trades), CUR3001(2 trades), FD4001(1 trade). `accounts.stream().map(Account::trades)` → `Stream<List<Trade>>` with 3 elements. Each element is a List, not a Trade. Cannot filter individual trades.

**Step 2 — flatMap.** `accounts.stream().flatMap(a -> a.trades().stream())` → each Account produces a `Stream<Trade>`, all three streams are merged into ONE `Stream<Trade>` with 6 elements. Now each trade is a top-level element.

**Step 3 — Process flat.** filter(amount > X), sort(by symbol), reduce(sum amounts), map(to symbols), distinct — all work on individual trades.

**Step 4 — Optional flatMap.** `trades.map(Trade::fee)` → `Stream<Optional<BigDecimal>>`. `flatMap(Optional::stream)` → present Optionals become values, empty Optionals vanish. 4 of 6 trades have fees → 4 BigDecimal values in flat stream.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ map() — ONE-TO-ONE (wraps) ═══

  Account SAV2001 ──map(::trades)──→ [T1, T2, T3]      ← List element
  Account CUR3001 ──map(::trades)──→ [T4, T5]           ← List element
  Account FD4001  ──map(::trades)──→ [T6]               ← List element
  Result: Stream<List<Trade>> = [[T1,T2,T3], [T4,T5], [T6]]  ← 3 elements!

  ═══ flatMap() — ONE-TO-MANY + FLATTEN (unwraps) ═══

  Account SAV2001 ──flatMap──→ T1, T2, T3     ← individual Trades
  Account CUR3001 ──flatMap──→ T4, T5         ← individual Trades
  Account FD4001  ──flatMap──→ T6             ← individual Trade
  Result: Stream<Trade> = [T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6]  ← 6 elements!

  ═══ flatMap WITH Optional ═══

  T1.fee = Optional.of(245)  ──flatMap(Optional::stream)──→ 245
  T2.fee = Optional.empty()  ──flatMap(Optional::stream)──→ (nothing)
  T3.fee = Optional.of(330)  ──flatMap(Optional::stream)──→ 330
  Result: Stream<BigDecimal> = [245, 330, 222, 124]  ← empties GONE!
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
map performs a one-to-one transformation: each element T produces exactly one element R. flatMap performs a one-to-many transformation and flattens: each element T produces a Stream of R values, and all streams are merged into a single flat Stream of R. The practical distinction: if map gives you Stream of List of Trade (nested), flatMap gives you Stream of Trade (flat). Use flatMap whenever you have nested structures — accounts with trades, orders with line items, lines with comma-separated values.

In my portfolio dashboard, map(Account::getTrades) produces Stream of List of Trade with 3 elements (three Lists). flatMap(a -> a.getTrades().stream()) produces Stream of Trade with 6 elements (six individual Trades). Only the flat stream allows filtering, sorting, and aggregating individual trades. I also demonstrate flatMap with Optional.stream (Java 9): map produces Stream of Optional of BigDecimal with empty entries; flatMap(Optional::stream) produces Stream of BigDecimal with only present values — empty Optionals are silently removed.

The signature makes the difference clear: map takes Function<T,R> and returns Stream<R>. flatMap takes Function<T, Stream<R>> — the function itself returns a Stream, and flatMap merges all those streams into one. flatMap can produce zero elements (Stream.empty()), one element (Stream.of(value)), or many elements — making it strictly more powerful than map. The rule of thumb: if you see Stream<List<T>>, Stream<Optional<T>>, or Stream<Stream<T>>, you need flatMap to unwrap the nesting.
